documentNotes.title: Native editorial preface
documentNotes.statement:
Preface
Preface
Preface
Preface 
This publication contains the competition problems (Volume 2) from the 21st – 40th 
International Chemistry Olympiads (IChO) organized in the years 1989 – 2008  and is a 
continuation of the publication that appeared last year as Volume 1 and contained 
competition problems from the first twenty IChOs.  The whole review of the competition 
tasks set in the IChO in its fourty-year history is a contribution of the IChO International 
Information Centre in Bratislava (Slovakia) to the development of this world known 
international competition. This Volume 2 contains 154 theoretical and 46 practical 
competition problems from the mentioned years. The review as a whole presents 
altogether 279 theoretical and 96 practical problems.  
In the elaboration of this collection the editor had to face certain difficulties because 
the aim was not only to make use of past recordings but also to give them such a form 
that they may be used in practice and further chemical education. Consequently, it was 
necessary to make some corrections in order to unify the form of the problems. However, 
they did not concern the contents and language of the problems.  
Unfortunately, the authors of the particular competition problems are not known and 
due to the procedure of the creation of the IChO competition problems, it is impossible to 
assign any author's name to a particular problem. As the editor I would appreciate many  
times some discussion with the authors about any critical places that occurred in the text. 
On the other hand, any additional amendments to the text would be not correct from the  
historical point of view. Therefore, responsibility for the scientific content and language of 
the problems lies exclusively with the organizers of the particular International Chemistry 
Olympiads.    
 
Some parts of texts, especially those gained as scanned materials, could not be 
used directly and thus, several texts, schemes and pictures had to be re-written or created 
again. Some solutions were often available in a brief form and necessary extent only, just 
for the needs of members of the International Jury.  
 
Recalculations of the solutions were made in some special cases only when the 
numeric results in the original solutions showed to be obviously not correct. Although the 
numbers of significant figures in the results of several solutions do not obey the criteria 
generally accepted, they were left without change.      


 
In this publication SI quantities and units are used and a more modern method of 
chemical calculations is introduced. Only some exceptions have been made when, in an 
effort to preserve the original text, the quantities and units have been used that are not SI.  
There were some problems with the presentation of the solutions of practical tasks, 
because most of the relatively simple calculations were based on the experimental results 
of contestants. Moreover, the practical problems are accompanied with answer sheets in 
the last years and several additional questions and tasks have appeared in them that were 
not a part of the text of the original experimental problems. Naturally, answer sheets could 
not be included in this publication and can only be preserved as archive materials. 
  
When reading the texts of the IChO problems one must admire and appreciate the 
work of those many known and unknown people – teachers, authors, pupils, and 
organizers – who contributed so much to development and success of this important 
international competition. 
 
I am sure about the usefulness of the this review of the IChO problems. It may serve 
not only as archive material but, in particular, this review should serve to both competitors 
and their teachers as a source of further inspiration in their preparation for this challenging 
competition. 
 
 
 
 
Bratislava, July 2009  
 
 
 
 
 
 
  
 
                                    Anton Sirota, editor

problems.title: Problem 1: Synthesis of Compounds with Wound Healing Properties
problems.statement:
Shikonin is a red compound found in the roots of the plant *Lithospermum erythrorhizon*, which grows in Asia. Extracts of the root have been used for centuries in folk medicine and are used today in ointments for healing wounds.

![](p1-fig1)

![](p1-fig2)

parts.statement: How many stereoisomers of Shikonin are possible?

Do all stereoisomers of Shikonin have the same melting point? Mark yes or no with an X.

The following sequence is part of a synthetic route to Shikonin:

![](p1-fig3)
Draw the structural formula of reagent A.

Indicate with an X in the appropriate check-box the correct IUPAC name for reagent A:

- ☐ 2-Methyl-2-pentenoyl chloride
- ☐ 1-Chloro-4-methyl-3-pentene
- ☐ 4-Methyl-3-pentenoyl chloride

problems.title: Problem 2: Bridge between Denmark and Sweden
problems.statement:
![](p2-fig1)

On July 1, 2000, the combined tunnel and bridge connecting Denmark and Sweden was officially opened. It consists of a tunnel from Copenhagen to an artificial island, and a bridge from the island to Malmö in Sweden. Its major construction materials are concrete and steel. This problem concerns chemical reactions relating to production and degradation of these materials.

Concrete is produced from cement, water, sand and small stones. Cement consists primarily of calcium silicates and calcium aluminates formed by heating and grinding clay and limestone. In the later production steps a small amount of gypsum, $\mathrm{CaSO_4\cdot2H_2O}$, improves subsequent hardening. Elevated temperatures during final production may form unwanted hemihydrate, $\mathrm{CaSO_4\cdot\tfrac12 H_2O}$:

$$
\mathrm{CaSO_4\cdot2H_2O(s)}\longrightarrow
\mathrm{CaSO_4\cdot\tfrac12 H_2O(s)}+\tfrac32\mathrm{H_2O(g)}.
$$

The following data apply at $25\,{}^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, standard pressure $1.00\,\mathrm{bar}$:

| Compound | $\Delta_f H^{\circ}$ / $\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$ | $S^{\circ}$ / $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}$ |
|---|---:|---:|
| $\mathrm{CaSO_4\cdot2H_2O(s)}$ | −2021.0 | 194.0 |
| $\mathrm{CaSO_4\cdot\tfrac12 H_2O(s)}$ | −1575.0 | 130.5 |
| $\mathrm{H_2O(g)}$ | −241.8 | 188.6 |

$R=8.314\,\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}}=0.08314\,\mathrm{L\,bar\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$; $0\,{}^{\circ}\mathrm{C}=273.15\,\mathrm{K}$.

parts.statement: Calculate $\Delta H^{\circ}$ in kJ for transformation of $1.00\,\mathrm{kg}$ of gypsum to hemihydrate. Is the reaction endothermic or exothermic?
Calculate the equilibrium water-vapour pressure in bar in a closed vessel containing gypsum, hemihydrate and water vapour at $25\,{}^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$.

Calculate the temperature at which the equilibrium water-vapour pressure is $1.00\,\mathrm{bar}$ in the system described in problem 2-2. Assume $\Delta H^{\circ}$ and $\Delta S^{\circ}$ are temperature independent.

sections.title: Corrosion of iron
sections.statement:
Metal corrosion involves electrochemical reactions. The initial electrode reactions forming rust on iron surfaces usually are

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{Fe(s)}&\longrightarrow\mathrm{Fe^{2+}(aq)}+2e^-,\\
\mathrm{O_2(g)}+2\mathrm{H_2O(l)}+4e^-&\longrightarrow4\mathrm{OH^-(aq)}.
\end{aligned}
$$

At $25\,{}^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ an electrochemical cell is represented by

$$
\mathrm{Fe(s)\mid Fe^{2+}(aq)\parallel OH^-(aq),O_2(g)\mid Pt(s)}.
$$

Standard reduction potentials are $E^{\circ}(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}/Fe})=-0.44\,\mathrm{V}$ and $E^{\circ}(\mathrm{O_2/OH^-})=0.40\,\mathrm{V}$. The Nernst factor is $RT\ln10/F=0.05916\,\mathrm{V}$ and $F=96485\,\mathrm{C\,mol^{-1}}$.

parts.statement: Calculate the standard electromotive force, $E^{\circ}$, at $25\,{}^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$.
Write the overall reaction during discharge under standard conditions.
Calculate the equilibrium constant at $25\,{}^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ for the overall cell reaction.

Allow the overall reaction to proceed for 24 hours under standard conditions at a constant current of $0.12\,\mathrm{A}$. Calculate the mass of Fe converted to $\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$. Oxygen and water are in excess.
Calculate $E$ at $25\,{}^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ for $[\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}]=0.015\,\mathrm{M}$, right-hand half-cell pH $9.00$, and $p(\mathrm{O_2})=0.700\,\mathrm{bar}$.

sections.statement:
$$
\Delta H^{\circ}=-1575.0+1.5(-241.8)-(-2021.0)=83.3\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}.
$$

$n=m/M=1000/172.18=5.808\,\mathrm{mol}$, so $\Delta H^{\circ}=484\,\mathrm{kJ}$. The reaction is endothermic.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Delta S^{\circ}&=130.5+\tfrac32(188.6)-194.0=219.4\,\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}},\\
\Delta G^{\circ}&=\Delta H^{\circ}-T\Delta S^{\circ}=17886\,\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}=-RT\ln K,\\
K&=p(\mathrm{H_2O})^{3/2}=7.35\times10^{-4},\\
p(\mathrm{H_2O})&=8.15\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{bar}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Pressure is expressed in bar.

$p(\mathrm{H_2O})=1.00\,\mathrm{bar}$ implies $K=1.00$ and $\Delta G^{\circ}=0$. The printed calculation is

$$0=83300\,\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}-T\,219.4\,\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}.$$

It gives $T=380\,\mathrm{K}$, or $107\,{}^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$.

Oxidation occurs in the negative left half-cell:

$$
\begin{aligned}
2\mathrm{Fe}&\longrightarrow2\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}+4e^-,\\
\mathrm{O_2}+2\mathrm{H_2O}+4e^-&\longrightarrow4\mathrm{OH^-},\\
2\mathrm{Fe}+\mathrm{O_2}+2\mathrm{H_2O}&\longrightarrow2\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}+4\mathrm{OH^-}.
\end{aligned}
$$

$$K=\frac{[\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}]^2[\mathrm{OH^-}]^4}{p(\mathrm{O_2})},\qquad \Delta G=-nFE(\text{cell})=-RT\ln K.$$

Concentrations are in M and pressure in bar. $K=6.2\times10^{56}$.

problems.title: Problem 3: Bioinorganic Chemistry
problems.statement: The square-planar complex cis-diammine dichloroplatinum(II) is an important drug for treating certain cancers.

parts.statement: Draw cis- and trans-diammine dichloroplatinum(II), and label each structure cis or trans.

Write molecular formulas for all ionic compounds with empirical formula $\mathrm{Pt(NH_3)_2Cl_2}$ satisfying all of these conditions:

1. The empirical formula is $\mathrm{Pt(NH_3)_2Cl_2}$.
2. The compound has an anion and a cation composed of discrete, monomeric square-planar platinum(II) complexes.
3. There is only one type of cation and one type of anion.

The answer must clearly reveal the composition of each discrete platinum(II) complex entity.

How many 5d electrons are in the platinum(II) ion?

The valence d-orbital splitting diagram of a square-planar complex may be derived from an octahedral complex: interactions with the two ligands on the z axis vanish, while bonds to the four remaining ligands on the x and y axes become stronger.
Which of the five 5d orbitals has the highest energy, and is thus least likely to be occupied, in a general square-planar Pt(II) complex?

sections.title: Iron binding by transferrin
sections.statement:
Serum transferrin (Tf) is a monomeric protein transporting iron(III) in the human body. Each molecule binds up to two iron(III) ions, with stepwise constants at biological conditions except for a temperature of $25\,{}^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{Fe^{III}}+\mathrm{Tf}&\longrightarrow(\mathrm{Fe^{III}})\mathrm{Tf},&K_1&=4.7\times10^{20},\\
\mathrm{Fe^{III}}+(\mathrm{Fe^{III}})\mathrm{Tf}&\longrightarrow(\mathrm{Fe^{III}})_2\mathrm{Tf},&K_2&=2.4\times10^{19}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The diferric protein has two similar but non-identical binding sites. The two monoferric forms are denoted $\{\mathrm{Fe^{III}\cdot Tf}\}$ and $\{\mathrm{Tf\cdot Fe^{III}}\}$, with

$$K=\frac{[\{\mathrm{Tf\cdot Fe^{III}}\}]}{[\{\mathrm{Fe^{III}\cdot Tf}\}]}=5.9.$$

parts.statement:
Calculate

$$K_1'=\frac{[\{\mathrm{Fe^{III}\cdot Tf}\}]}{[\mathrm{Fe^{III}}][\mathrm{Tf}]},\qquad K_1''=\frac{[\{\mathrm{Tf\cdot Fe^{III}}\}]}{[\mathrm{Fe^{III}}][\mathrm{Tf}]}.$$

Calculate

$$K_2'=\frac{[(\mathrm{Fe^{III}})_2\mathrm{Tf}]}{[\mathrm{Fe^{III}}][\{\mathrm{Fe^{III}\cdot Tf}\}]},\qquad K_2''=\frac{[(\mathrm{Fe^{III}})_2\mathrm{Tf}]}{[\mathrm{Fe^{III}}][\{\mathrm{Tf\cdot Fe^{III}}\}]}.$$

Each bound iron(III) ion is surrounded by six donor atoms: two oxygens of carbonate and one potential donor atom from each of one aspartate, one histidine and two tyrosine side chains.
What is the total number of oxygen donor atoms around a six-coordinate iron(III) ion in transferrin?

sections.statement: The $5d_{x^2-y^2}$ orbital. The four ligand atoms lie on the x and y axes, along which this orbital would have concentrated electron density if occupied.

The total monoferric concentration is the sum of the two forms. Thus

$$K_1'+K_1''=K_1,\qquad K_1'K=K_1''.$$

$$K_1'=\frac{K_1}{1+K}=\frac{4.7\times10^{20}}{1+5.9}=6.8\times10^{19},\qquad K_1''=K_1-K_1'=(4.7-0.68)10^{20}=4.0\times10^{20}.$$

$$K_1'K_2'=K_1''K_2''=K_1K_2.$$

The first printed substitution is labelled $K_1'$:

$$K_1'=\frac{K_1K_2}{K_1'}=\frac{4.7\times10^{20}\times2.19\times10^{19}}{6.8\times10^{19}}=1.7\times10^{20}.$$

The second is

$$K_1''K_2''=K_1K_2,\qquad K_2''=\frac{K_1K_2}{K_1''}=\frac{4.7\times10^{20}\times2.4\times10^{19}}{4.0\times10^{20}}=2.8\times10^{19}.$$

problems.title: Problem 4: A Naturally Occurring Compound
problems.statement: A naturally occurring compound A contains only C, H and O, with mass percentages C: 63.2%, H: 5.3%, O: 31.5%.

parts.statement:
Derive the empirical formula of A.

![](p4-fig1)

Figure 1 is the mass spectrum of compound A.

What is the molecular formula of A?

A solution of A in ether is shaken with aqueous NaOH. Afterwards no A remains in the ether phase. Another solution in ether is shaken with aqueous $\mathrm{NaHCO_3}$, and A remains in the ether phase.

Which classes does A belong to according to these experiments? Mark with an X: ☐ alcohol; ☐ phenol; ☐ aldehyde; ☐ ketone; ☐ acid; ☐ ester; ☐ ether.

A gives a silver mirror with Tollens' reagent, $\mathrm{Ag(NH_3)_2^+}$.

Which functional groups does this indicate in A? Mark with an X: ☐ hydroxy group of an alcohol; ☐ hydroxy group of a phenol; ☐ carbonyl group of an aldehyde; ☐ carbonyl group of a ketone; ☐ carboxylic group; ☐ ester group; ☐ alkoxy group of an ether.

sections.title: NMR evidence
sections.statement:
![](p4-fig2)

The $^1\mathrm{H}$ NMR spectrum was recorded at 300 MHz: solvent $\mathrm{CDCl_3}$ (7.27 ppm), reference tetramethylsilane. The signals at 3.9, 6.3 and 9.8 ppm are singlets. Figure 2b expands the region 6.9–7.6 ppm.

![](p4-fig3)

Selected shifts and coupling constants are in Table 1 below. The signal at 6.3 ppm disappears on adding a drop of $\mathrm{D_2O}$.

parts.statement:
What does this indicate? Mark with an X: ☐ exchange of carbon-bonded hydrogen; ☐ exchange of oxygen-bonded hydrogen; ☐ dilution effect; ☐ hydrolysis.

The same signal moves to a lower ppm value on dilution with $\mathrm{CDCl_3}$.
Indicate all true statements: ☐ increased hydrogen bonding; ☐ decrease in hydrogen bonding; ☐ intermolecular hydrogen bonding; ☐ intramolecular hydrogen bonding; ☐ no hydrogen bonding.
Draw the four possible structural formulas for A based on the information above.
Give structural formulas of the fragments lost corresponding to peaks at 137 and 123 mass units in the mass spectrum.
Two isomers have lower $pK_a$ values than the others. Write their formulas.

problems.title: Problem 5: Protein and DNA
problems.statement:
![](p5-fig1)

DNA is composed of 2′-deoxynucleotides carrying adenine (A), guanine (G), cytosine (C) and thymine (T). Table 2 gives the molar masses of the 2′-deoxynucleotide-5′-triphosphates:

| dNTP | Molar mass / $\mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}$ |
|---|---:|
| dATP | 487 |
| dGTP | 503 |
| dCTP | 464 |
| dTTP | 478 |

parts.statement:
Calculate the molar mass of a double-stranded DNA fragment of 1000 base pairs with a uniform distribution of all four bases.

PCR (polymerase chain reaction) can isolate and clone this fragment: a heat-stable DNA polymerase cyclically multiplies a specific DNA piece. Under optimal conditions each cycle doubles the number of double-stranded copies. Perform 30 cycles starting with a single double-stranded DNA molecule.

Calculate the approximate mass of the DNA obtained.

The bacteria-virus T4 enzyme polynucleotide kinase (PNK) transfers ATP's terminal phosphate ($\gamma$-orthophosphate) to the 5′-hydroxyl termini of ribo- and deoxyribonucleotides:

![](p5-fig2)

PNK labels DNA at the 5′ end with $^{32}\mathrm{P}$, using ATP whose outermost ($\gamma$) phosphorus is replaced by $^{32}\mathrm{P}$. Its amount, and hence labelled DNA, can be measured.

A $10\,\mu\mathrm{L}$ solution of double-stranded DNA is labelled 100% with $[\gamma\text{-}^{32}\mathrm{P}]\mathrm{ATP}$ by PNK. Thirty-seven days ago its specific activity was $10\,\mathrm{Ci\,mmol^{-1}}$, or $370\times10^9\,\mathrm{Bq\,mmol^{-1}}$. The half-life is 14.2 days; each decay emits a $\beta$ particle. Now the labelled DNA emits 40000 $\beta$ particles per second.

Calculate the concentration of the DNA solution.

PNK incubated with $[\gamma\text{-}^{32}\mathrm{P}]\mathrm{ATP}$ and single-stranded DNA can be monitored by isolating labelled DNA and measuring $\beta$ emission. In a $1\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ mixture this gives labelling of $9\,\mathrm{nmol\,min^{-1}}$. PNK has turnover number $0.05\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ and molar mass $34620\,\mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}$.
Calculate PNK concentration in $\mathrm{mg\,cm^{-3}}$.

sections.title: Aromatic amino acids
sections.statement: Tryptophan, tyrosine and phenylalanine absorb UV between 240 and 300 nm. In a protein their summed amino-acid molar absorptivities approximately equal the protein's molar absorptivity. At 280 nm, the respective values for tyrosine, tryptophan and phenylalanine are 1400, 5600 and $5\,\mathrm{M^{-1}\,cm^{-1}}$. A $10\,\mu\mathrm{M}$ PNK solution has absorbance 0.644 at 280 nm and path length 1.00 cm. PNK contains 14 tyrosines and 9 phenylalanines. Here $\mathrm{M}=\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$.

parts.statement: Calculate the number of tryptophan residues per PNK molecule.

sections.statement:
$2^{30}=1073741824$ copies. The printed mass calculation uses

$$m(\mathrm{DNA})=\frac{1073741824}{N_A}\times616350\,\mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}=1.1\,\mathrm{ng}.$$

$$A=A_0e^{-kt},\qquad k=\frac{\ln2}{t_{1/2}},\qquad A_0=\frac{40000}{e^{-0.0488\times37}}=243464\,\mathrm{dps}.$$

This corresponds to $243464/370=658\,\mathrm{pmol}$ of 5′-$^{32}\mathrm{P}$-DNA. Since the volume is $10\,\mu\mathrm{L}$, its concentration is approximately $66\,\mu\mathrm{M}$.

problems.title: Problem 6: Hard Water
problems.statement:
Denmark's subsoil is mainly limestone. Groundwater containing carbon dioxide dissolves some calcium carbonate as calcium hydrogen carbonate. This makes the water hard; as tap water it precipitates calcium carbonate in kitchens and bathrooms.

Carbon dioxide is a diprotic acid in water. At $0\,{}^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{CO_2(aq)}+\mathrm{H_2O(l)}&\rightleftharpoons\mathrm{HCO_3^-(aq)}+\mathrm{H^+(aq)},&pK_{a1}&=6.630,\\
\mathrm{HCO_3^-(aq)}&\rightleftharpoons\mathrm{CO_3^{2-}(aq)}+\mathrm{H^+(aq)},&pK_{a2}&=10.640.
\end{aligned}
$$

Neglect liquid-volume changes from dissolving $\mathrm{CO_2}$ throughout. All temperatures are $0\,{}^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$.

parts.statement: At $p(\mathrm{CO_2})=1.00\,\mathrm{bar}$ the total carbon-dioxide concentration in saturated water is $0.0752\,\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$. Calculate the gas volume dissolved in one litre of water. $R=8.314\,\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}}=0.08314\,\mathrm{L\,bar\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$.
Calculate the equilibrium concentrations of hydrogen ions and $\mathrm{CO_2}$ in water saturated at $p(\mathrm{CO_2})=1.00\,\mathrm{bar}$.
Calculate the equilibrium hydrogen-ion concentration in $0.0100\,\mathrm{M}$ aqueous sodium hydrogen carbonate saturated at $p(\mathrm{CO_2})=1.00\,\mathrm{bar}$.
Calculate the equilibrium hydrogen-ion concentration in $0.0100\,\mathrm{M}$ aqueous sodium carbonate saturated at $p(\mathrm{CO_2})=1.00\,\mathrm{bar}$. Ignore water dissociation.
Calcium carbonate's solubility is $0.0012\,\mathrm{g}$ per $100\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of water. Calculate the calcium-ion concentration in its saturated aqueous solution.

sections.title: Hard groundwater
sections.statement:
Groundwater reacts with limestone and dissolved carbon dioxide:

$$\mathrm{CaCO_3(s)}+\mathrm{CO_2(aq)}+\mathrm{H_2O(l)}\rightleftharpoons\mathrm{Ca^{2+}(aq)}+2\mathrm{HCO_3^-(aq)}.$$

The equilibrium constant is $K=10^{-4.25}$ at $0\,{}^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$.

parts.statement: Calculate calcium-ion concentration in water equilibrated with calcium carbonate in an atmosphere with carbon-dioxide partial pressure $1.00\,\mathrm{bar}$.
A $0.0150\,\mathrm{M}$ calcium-hydroxide solution is saturated with carbon dioxide at $1.00\,\mathrm{bar}$. Calculate calcium-ion concentration using the equilibrium in part 6.6.

Dilute the part 6.7 calcium-hydroxide solution to twice its volume before saturating with carbon dioxide at $1.00\,\mathrm{bar}$. Calculate calcium-ion concentration in the resulting saturated solution.
Calculate calcium carbonate's solubility-product constant from the data above.

sections.statement:
The key prints $0.0012\,\mathrm{g}$ of $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ in $100\,\mathrm{cm^3}$, followed by

$$0.0012\,\mathrm{g}\,/100\times0872\,\mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}=0.000012\,\mathrm{mol\ CaCO_3}\text{ in }100\,\mathrm{cm^3}\text{ of water}.$$

$[\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}]=1.2\times10^{-4}$; $c(\mathrm{Ca^{2+}})=1.2\times10^{-4}\,\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$.

$c(\mathrm{Ca(OH)_2})=0.015\,\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$ and $\mathrm{OH^-+CO_2\to HCO_3^-}$. All hydroxide has been consumed ($K=10^{7.37}$). Part 6.6 gives a smaller maximum calcium concentration, so $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ precipitates. $[\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}]=1.02\times10^{-2}$; $c=1.02\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$.

$c(\mathrm{Ca(OH)_2})=0.0075\,\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$, below the maximum $1.02\times10^{-2}$ from 6.6. No calcium carbonate precipitates; $[\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}]=0.75\times10^{-2}$ and $c=0.75\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}}$.

problems.statementAfterParts:
### Source notes

The native 6.5 line prints “/100 × 0872 g mol−1”; the malformed expression is retained rather than reconstructed. Parts 6.6 and 6.9 omit a square on hydrogen carbonate; 6.6 also prints $4[\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}]/0.0751$ without a cubic exponent. Their printed numerical results are retained.
